newsitem.title: LEBANON: Limits on media unites Lebanese opposition.
newsitem.headline: Limits on media unites Lebanese opposition.

text.p: Hundreds of opposition figures accused Lebanon's pro-Syrian government of gagging the media and demanded cancellation of a law slashing the number of private television and radio stations.

Some 700 trade unionists, parliamentary deputies, media workers and politicians met on Wednesday night. They appointed a committee that will meet next Monday to draft a plan, including strikes, demonstrations and sit-ins, to force the government to bow to their demands.

Under the law the government has licenced four private television stations and 11 radio stations, putting dozens of television stations and scores of radio stations out of business and thousands of people out of work.

Three of the four licenced television stations are owned by prominent government figures, including billionaire Prime Minister Rafik al-Hariri. Of the three radio stations allowed to broadcast news, two are owned by the same people.

Newspapers said the "National Meeting for the Defence of Freedoms" was an unprecedented gathering of the Lebanese opposition that could be the first sign of a move to form a national opposition front.
Many participants and political parties present were former enemies or rivals from different religious sects who had rarely if ever taken joint action.

They included prominent conservative Sunni Moslem politicians side-by-side with radical pro-Iranian Shi'ites of Hizbollah (Party of God) and Christian opposition deputies recently elected to parliament beside prominent nationalist Christians who boycotted the polls.
Representatives of exiled nationalist Christian leaders were also present.

Former prime minister Selim al-Hoss, a parliamentary deputy, said the law served the twin purposes of satisfying the personal interests of Lebanon's rulers and gagging opposition media. He said the number of televisions should be increased to 10.

Former information minister Michel Samaha, a Greek Catholic now in opposition who failed to win election to parliament last month, said Lebanon was now facing "the dictatorial values of Third World countries."

Firebrand Greek Orthodox Najah Wakim, Hariri's most bitter critic in parliament, said Lebanon was dying through the loss of its liberties and sovereignty under the pro-Syrian government that Hariri heads.
